newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Jerusalem market bombs could mark Islamist rift.
newsitem.headline: Jerusalem market bombs could mark Islamist rift.

text.p: Twin suicide bombs that killed 13 people in a Jewish market in Jerusalem on Wednesday could signal a rift between local Islamist leaders and rivals in exile, according to political analysts.
Some Israeli newspapers on Friday reported that the bombers may have come from abroad.

"I think most of the leaders on the inside have abandoned the notion that violence pays and most have been willing to become part of the (Palestinian) political process," Palestinian political analyst Khalil Shkaki said.
If the bombings were organised abroad "it could deepen the split -- this order from the outside without consulting the inside", he said.
The bombings were the first in Israel since March and the bloodiest in more than a year.
A leaflet issued after the bombing claimed the attack in the name of the militant group Hamas, though an Israeli official has said investigators are not certain it is authentic.
If Hamas is responsible it could be a sign that the movement, which wants to replace Israel with an Islamic state, is at war with itself, Shkaki said.
If the Islamic Jihad group is responsible, that shows it has stopped discriminating between military and civilian targets, he added.
Hamas leaders abroad want to continue a war to the death with the Jewish state, but those in the West Bank and Gaza are starting to get involved in the political process.
"I don't know if (local Hamas leaders) will be able to come out and condemn this violence, but I doubt you will find one mainstream Hamas leader who supports this action," Shkaki said.
"You will find one in Amman, but not here," he said.
Though at odds, the two Hamas factions need each other. Locals need funds from abroad and exiled leaders depend on those in Palestinian areas for political legitimacy, said Israeli analyst Anat Kurz.
She also said the attack could have been masterminded abroad.
Local leaders are more concerned with easing poverty in the Palestinian territories, where the average daily wage ranges from $11 to $28 a day.
Hamas social services support thousands of poor families in the Gaza Strip alone and employ hundreds of workers. They sponsor a women's movement, labour unions and schools.
"We think sometimes this is better than the military attacks," Islamist editor and Hamas leader Ghazi Hamad said in an interview a week before the bombing.
Hamas formed out of the political and social Moslem Brotherhood at the start of the Palestinian intifada (uprising) against Israeli occupation to pursue armed struggle against the Jewish state.
Islamic Jihad is much older. It broke away from the Brothers years before the intifada back when the Brotherhood wanted to stop violence.
Based in Damascus, it has strong links to Iran, where it gets money, training and ideological support, Shkaki said.
Although they have similar ideology, Hamas, unlike Islamic Jihad, has primarily targeted civilians in its attacks.
"Islamic Jihad used to be more discriminating in their targets. They used to hit military instead of civilian targets," Shkaki said.
Both organisations depend on their social services for local support, though Hamas has a stronger base.

That foundation was weakened when Yasser Arafat's Palestinian Authority cracked down after a series of suicide bombs killed 57 people in 1996, arresting more than 900 Hamas and Islamic Jihad activists. Many of them were later released.

"It taught them a lesson that if they continue violence, they risk the existence of their organisation. They put at risk their whole political and social infrastructure, not just their military infrastructure," Shkaki said.
"They have to give up violence, and I think they've made that switch," he said.
